analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health plan covering every American, replacing Medicare, Medicaid, and most private coverage.
analysis.headline: The bill received no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Bernie Sanders' bill would have given every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident free choice of doctors with no premiums, deductibles, or copays, funded by taxes instead of insurance bills. It would have replaced Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee coverage, and military coverage with state-run programs, and it would have banned the sale of private insurance that duplicates those benefits. Every action on the bill was one line: it was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident who is a citizen, national, or lawful resident alien would be entitled to hospital care, doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care with no charge for covered services and no balance billing. Small businesses now paying rising health premiums would stop carrying that cost, since the bill's own findings cite employers' health bills rising 10-15% a year as a drag on hiring.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Every citizen, national, and lawful resident alien is entitled to comprehensive health benefits under a state health security program, with automatic enrollment at birth and at legal immigration.

Covered benefits include inpatient and outpatient hospital care, professional services, prescription drugs, dental care, mental health and substance abuse treatment, preventive services, and home and community-based long-term care.
Providers in the program may not charge patients for covered services, and balance billing is prohibited.

The bill's findings state that U.S. health spending is nearly double the next most costly nation's, that 51 million Americans were uninsured in 2009, and that small businesses face health bills rising 10-15% a year.

analysis.who_pays: Employers pay a new payroll tax, individuals pay a health care income tax, high earners pay a surcharge, and securities transactions are taxed, with all proceeds flowing to a new American Health Security Trust Fund. The health insurance industry loses its core business: Medicare, Medicaid, and employer-based private coverage are wound down, and selling insurance that duplicates the program is banned.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates benefits under Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and TRICARE after December 31, 2012, replacing programs tens of millions of people use today with newly built state-run systems, a transition the bill itself acknowledges carries risk by continuing in-stay hospital benefits only until the stay ends.
Financing rests on new taxes: a payroll tax on employers, a health care income tax, a surcharge on high-income individuals, and a tax on securities transactions.

States must prohibit the sale of health insurance that duplicates program benefits, so people could no longer buy a private plan for covered care, a choice restriction that is the point of the bill but a real cost to those who prefer private coverage.

Hospitals would be paid through approved global budgets and practitioners through a prospective fee schedule, a fundamental change that hospitals and physician groups have historically fought because it caps their revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is the largest possible in health policy: everyone covered, no out-of-pocket charges for covered care, and the end of medical bills as a cause of bankruptcy. The costs are equally real: a multi-trillion-dollar shift of health spending onto the tax system, the dismantling of five existing programs that people rely on, and a ban on duplicate private coverage. The honest objection is not that the goals are wrong but that the transition was never worked through with anyone: the bill had no cosponsors, no committee hearing, and no cost estimate, so the financing and the wind-down of Medicare and Medicaid were never stress-tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never scheduled it for a hearing or a vote, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on May 9, 2011; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
That was the bill's entire action history: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote during the two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The health insurance industry kept its role in the health system, and hospitals and employers kept the existing payment and coverage arrangements. No one gained expanded coverage; the roughly 51 million uninsured figure cited in the bill's findings remained unaddressed by this bill, with the Affordable Care Act's exchange system continuing instead of being repealed as the bill proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the existing system

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the single-payer bill and was its only sponsor; no colleague joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the remainder of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee holding the bill, never scheduled it for consideration; committee chairs decide whether referred bills get a markup or hearing.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and the bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured; single-payer bills in this era drew support almost exclusively from the left flank while mainstream members of both parties avoided them.

industries.note: The bill repeals the Affordable Care Act's exchange framework, winds down Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, FEHB, and TRICARE, and bans the sale of any insurance that duplicates program benefits, eliminating the industry's core market. Its survival depended on the bill dying, and it did.

Hospitals would be paid through approved global budgets and practitioners through a prospective fee schedule, ending balance billing and capping facility revenue. In exchange they would get a universal payer, ending uncompensated care for the uninsured.
Prescription drugs would be paid under a board-set payment schedule rather than negotiated market prices, and a single national program would have far more bargaining power than fragmented insurers.

Employers would pay a new payroll tax but shed premium contributions; the bill's findings argue employer health costs rising 10-15% a year are a drag on job creation. Employee benefit plans duplicating coverage would be prohibited.
A tax on securities transactions would help fund the trust fund, a direct though modest cost to trading firms and high-volume investors.
